abstract: The paper introduces narrative-level streaming virality prediction as a new task for misinformation triage, motivated by the gap between how fast false narratives peak (median 1.5 days) and how slowly fact-checks arrive (median 4.5 days). It presents an end-to-end streaming pipeline with four main stages: online clustering of semantically equivalent posts into evolving narratives, kernel-density anomaly detection over cluster activity, LLM-based claim normalization, and cluster-level spread prediction via a novel Post-Detection Spread Ratio (PSR) metric, followed by an interpretable check-worthiness classifier. The authors release the first dataset and baselines for the new task, built from a 1.52M-post US political-event Twitter/X stream, and show state-of-the-art results on two established Automatic Claim Detection tasks.
key_claims: The natural unit of analysis for fact-checking triage is the narrative (a cluster of semantically equivalent claims), not individual posts or coarse events, which prior virality work targets.
Automatic Claim Detection should extend beyond static classification to support pre-virality, claim-level streaming analysis grounded in journalistic decision criteria.
A novel Post-Detection Spread Ratio (PSR) metric quantifies the remaining intervention window at detection time and enables actionable triage before peak virality.
Task-specific prompting design (contrastive, topic-aware few-shot) matters more than raw model capacity for constrained claim normalization.

Interpretable architectures aligned with journalistic pre-judgment criteria (checkability, verifiability, harm potential) can match or exceed black-box fusion while generalizing better across datasets.
A distilled modular pipeline outperforms a frontier LLM (zero-shot) at check-worthiness at substantially lower cost and latency.
methods: Constructed a new dataset from the US Election 2020 Tweets Kaggle corpus (Oct 15–Nov 08, 2020), yielding 1.52M tweets after preprocessing, chosen for not needing hydration and for having collection-time engagement counts enabling no-lookahead temporal statistics.

Streaming clustering using paraphrase-multilingual-mpnet-base-v2 embeddings with incremental cosine-similarity clustering (threshold tau=0.65, O(n*k) time), after a claim gate (4–125 words, excluding reaction commentary).

Online anomaly detection with EXPoSE (Random Kitchen Sinks / kernel density via random Fourier features, D=20000, gamma=0.5, decay alpha=0.01, threshold 0.1), selected from NAB benchmark leaderboard, monitoring hourly tweet count and engagement.

Claim normalization via two-stage retrieval (multilingual-e5-base embeddings, post-to-post then claim-to-post verification) plus contrastive, topic-aware few-shot prompting with Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, Mixtral-8x7B, and DeepSeek-3.1v; evaluated with METEOR on the CT2025 English N=300 subset.

Virality prediction formulated as predicting PSR = (E_final - E_detect)/E_final, using 42 features from a 6-hour post-detection window; baselines across linear (Ridge, BayesianRidge), tree (RandomForest, LightGBM), kernel (SVR), sequence/point-process (LSTM, GRU, Hawkes), and text (BERTweet) models on 529 clusters with 80/20 split.

Check-worthiness classification with a 4-Parallel-Heads DeBERTa-v3-large (full 435M-parameter fine-tuning) decomposing into checkability, verifiability, harm potential, and overall heads, trained with class-weighted cross-entropy and LLM-derived soft labels (mistral-small-24b) via a three-phase schedule on cleaned CheckThat! 2024 Task 1 English splits.
Frontier-LLM zero-shot ablation with Claude Opus 4.7 on CT24 test-gold (N=341) with McNemar significance testing, plus cost/latency comparison.
Formative evaluation with six professional fact-checkers rating 18 claim-report pairs.
findings: On CT2025 English claim normalization (N=300), contrastive few-shot Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 reaches METEOR 0.5569, exceeding the strongest published baseline (0.4569) by 10.0 METEOR points and outperforming the larger Mixtral-8x7B (0.5463).

The 4-Parallel-Heads DeBERTa-v3-large achieves F1=0.833 on CheckThat! 2024 (vs prior SOTA 0.802), generalizing zero-shot to ClaimBuster (F1=0.973) and CheckThat! 2023 (F1=0.933); a late-fusion variant reaches marginally higher CT2024 F1 (0.836) but generalizes worse.
EXPoSE dominates classical detectors (NAB 79.2, 97.9% detected before peak, median +23h lead) because claim clusters violate stationarity assumptions.

Cluster-level virality is approximately linear: regularized linear (BayesianRidge rho=0.551) and kernel (SVR R2=0.336, MAE=0.207, best F2@0.65=0.632) models match or beat sequence models and point processes, which perform near-random; user/network authority features dominate over content features.
86% of check-worthiness errors are shared across approaches, indicating representation learning rather than feature engineering is the bottleneck.
Claude Opus 4.7 zero-shot trails the distilled classifier by 0.11 F1 (0.722 vs 0.833, McNemar p<10^-2) at ~$18/1k claims and ~9.9s latency versus <10ms and near-zero amortized cost.

The pipeline surfaces ~500 fact-check candidates from ~1.5M posts over three weeks, a triage ratio manageable by a small newsroom; fact-checkers agreed/partially agreed with recommendations in 83.3% of cases and all six rated the report structure aligned with practice.
Fine-tuning underperforms prompting for normalization (0.4427), and normalized claims can contain factual misstatements that METEOR does not penalize.
contributions: A new task formulation: narrative-level streaming virality prediction, with the narrative cluster as the unit of analysis.

The first dataset and baselines for this task: virality labels and 42-feature inputs for 529 anomalous cluster instances (535 distinct claims) from a 1.52M-post US political-event Twitter/X stream, plus code and prompts.
The novel Post-Detection Spread Ratio (PSR) metric quantifying the remaining intervention window at detection time.
State-of-the-art results on two established ACD tasks (CT2025 claim normalization and CheckThat! 2024 check-worthiness) proposed as new baselines.
An interpretable 4-Parallel-Heads architecture decomposing check-worthiness into checkability, verifiability, and harm potential, aligned with journalistic pre-judgment criteria.
A frontier-LLM zero-shot ablation and formative study with professional fact-checkers supporting the modular, distilled design.
framing: The work sits at the intersection of virality prediction, claim normalization, check-worthiness detection, and explainable fact-checking, positioning itself against prior ACD research that treats claim selection as static post-hoc classification. It frames the problem through journalism research on fact-checkers' multi-stage cognitive decision process under time and attention constraints, and against streaming misinformation detection work (e.g., IC-Mamba, narrative-emergence prediction) that operates on posts or discourse networks rather than canonical claim clusters.
